cat > .github/workflows/triage.yml <<'EOF'
---
name: triage

# pull_request_target runs in the context of the base repository, so the token
# can write to pull requests opened from forks. This workflow never checks out
# or executes code from the pull request, and it passes untrusted values (the
# title and author) through environment variables rather than interpolating
# them into the script.
on:
  pull_request_target:
    types: [opened]

permissions: {}

jobs:
  triage:
    name: Welcome and label
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 5
    permissions:
      pull-requests: write
      issues: write
    env:
      GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
      GH_REPO: ${{ github.repository }}
      PR_NUMBER: ${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
      PR_AUTHOR: ${{ github.event.pull_request.user.login }}
      PR_TITLE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}
    steps:
      - name: Ensure the needs-triage label exists
        run: gh label create needs-triage --description "Awaiting triage" --color FBCA04 || true

      - name: Apply the needs-triage label
        run: gh pr edit "$PR_NUMBER" --add-label needs-triage

      - name: Post the welcome comment
        run: |
          printf 'Welcome @%s, and thanks for your contribution!\n\nSummary: "%s"\n\nA maintainer will triage this pull request soon.\n' \
            "$PR_AUTHOR" "$PR_TITLE" > comment.md
          gh pr comment "$PR_NUMBER" --body-file comment.md
EOF
cat >> README.md <<'EOF'

## Triage workflow

`.github/workflows/triage.yml` runs when a pull request is opened. It:

- posts a comment welcoming the author by username and repeating the pull request title as a summary, and
- applies the `needs-triage` label (creating it if it does not exist).

Because contributions arrive from forks, the workflow uses the `pull_request_target` trigger. A plain `pull_request` run from a fork gets a read-only token and could not comment or label. The trade-off is that the workflow runs with write permissions, so it must never check out or run code from the pull request. It only calls the `gh` CLI, and it passes the title and username through environment variables rather than interpolating them into shell code, so a crafted title cannot inject commands. Keep it that way when editing.
EOF

content.text:
I added `.github/workflows/triage.yml` and a "Triage workflow" section in the README. I haven't run the workflow, because it needs a real pull request on GitHub.

- **What it does:** when a pull request is opened, it applies the `needs-triage` label. It creates the label first if the repo doesn't have it. It then posts a comment that welcomes `@<username>`, repeats the title as `Summary: "<title>"`, and says a maintainer will triage it soon.
- **Forks:** the workflow uses `pull_request_target`, not `pull_request`. A fork's `pull_request` run gets a read-only token and couldn't comment or label. With `pull_request_target` the token has `pull-requests: write` and `issues: write`.
- **Safety:** `pull_request_target` runs with write access, so the workflow never checks out or runs code from the pull request. It only uses the `gh` CLI, which comes with the runner, so there are no third-party actions to pin. The title and username are passed in as environment variables instead of being written into the shell script, so a title like `"; rm -rf` can't inject commands. The README says to keep it that way when editing.
